desc:
A rooted tree has n nodes numbered 0..n-1. It is described by an array parent where parent[v] is the parent of node v, and the single root has parent[root] = -1. The root can be any node, and a parent may have a larger number than its child.

The subtree size of a node is the number of nodes in the subtree hanging below it, counting the node itself. Return an array sizes where sizes[v] is the subtree size of node v.

parent = [1, -1, 1, 0, 0]

node 1 is the root with children 0 and 2; node 0 has children 3 and 4
sizes  = [3, 5, 1, 1, 1]
constraints: parent[v] = -1 for exactly one node (the root); every other entry is a node number in 0..n-1
The array describes a valid tree (following parents from any node reaches the root)
hints: Walking up from every node and adding one to each ancestor works but can take O(n<sup>2</sup>) on a long chain.
A node's size is 1 plus the sizes of its children. So children must be finished before their parent.

Build the list of children of each node, get an order in which every parent appears before its children (BFS from the root), then go through that order backwards, adding each node's size to its parent.
editorial: The size of a subtree obeys size[v] = 1 + sum(size[c] for c in children[v]). The values only depend on the children, so we need an order that processes a node after all of its descendants.

Build children from the parent array, run a BFS from the root to get an order where parents come first, then sweep that order in reverse and add size[v] to size[parent[v]]. Because the parent array does not guarantee parent[v] < v, a simple left-to-right sweep over indices would not be correct, which is why the BFS order is needed. A recursive DFS gives the same result but may overflow the call stack on a chain of 100,000 nodes.
Every node is visited a constant number of times: O(n) time and O(n) space.
